h1: When your customer's AI agent calls: how to prepare your business for AI agents
answer_first: To prepare your business for AI agents that act for your customers, decide three things before they show up: how you recognize an agent and the person it represents, what an agent may do with and without the customer signed in, and where a person takes over. Then put your facts, prices and policies in a form a machine can read, and log every agent request the way you log a human one.
body_html:
To prepare your business for AI agents that act for your customers, decide three things before they show up: how you recognize an agent and the person it represents, what an agent may do with and without the customer signed in, and where a person takes over. Then put your facts, prices and policies in a form a machine can read, and log every agent request the way you log a human one.

Until recently this was a thought experiment. Your AI agent answered your customers. Now your customers have agents of their own, and those agents are starting to call, chat and connect to your systems on the customer's behalf.

What changed recently?

Three developments in the past few months moved personal agents from demos to something a business has to plan for.

  • Consumer agents launched at scale. Meta released Muse in the US in September 2026, an agent that can send emails, book travel, fill out forms and make purchases for its user, with explicit approval available for sensitive actions such as purchases (TechRepublic, September 2026).
  • A shared standard was proposed. On October 6, 2026, Sierra and Meta announced the Personal Agent Protocol, an open standard for how personal agents sign in, identify themselves and complete tasks with companies. Genesys, Shopify, Stripe and Walmart are among the named partners (Sierra).
  • A first draft is public. Draft 0.1 of the specification is online, and it says plainly that any part of it can still change (Personal Agent Protocol spec). A few days later, insurers including GEICO, Liberty Mutual and Cigna were named among 35 new design partners (Coverager, October 2026).

Phone calls from machines are not new either. Since July 2025, Google Search has been able to call local businesses for its users to ask about prices and availability (Search Engine Journal).

Customers seem willing to hand this work over. In a Gartner survey of 4,879 customers in early 2025, 51% said they would be willing to let a generative AI assistant handle customer service interactions for them (Gartner, June 2025).

How does a customer's AI agent reach your business?

A personal AI agent reaches a business in one of three ways today.

RouteWhat it looks like to youWhat tends to go wrong
Your website, clicked through like a personOrdinary web traffic, sometimes flagged as a botForms change, captchas block it, the agent gives up or picks the wrong option
Your phone line or web chatA polite caller asking for prices, hours or a booking for someone elseNo way to verify who it acts for, long calls, staff unsure what they may share
A direct connectionA signed request to your APIs, an MCP server or your own AI agentNeeds work on your side first: identity, permissions and a list of what you offer

Sierra's announcement describes the second route as the fallback when the first one fails: agents "may call the company's support line or open its web chat," which can take a long time and may still not finish the task.

The Personal Agent Protocol is an attempt to make the third route normal. In the draft, a company publishes one file at /.well-known/poppy.json that tells agents how to start a session, how customers sign in and which routes the company offers: its website, its APIs (OpenAPI or MCP), or a conversation with the company's own agent.

How do you know who an agent is acting for?

There are two separate questions, and businesses tend to blur them. Which agent is this? And which customer gave it permission?

Agent identity is being solved with cryptography. Visa's Trusted Agent Protocol has agents sign their web requests with HTTP Message Signatures (RFC 9421), bound to the merchant's domain and the specific operation, so a merchant can reject replayed or relayed requests (Visa on GitHub). The Personal Agent Protocol draft takes a similar line: each agent publishes signing keys at a URL, signs its token requests, and binds its session tokens to a key it holds. Companies can allowlist, blocklist or rate-limit agents.

Customer permission runs on OAuth in the Personal Agent Protocol draft. A session starts signed out. The company knows which agent is asking but not who the person is, which is enough for questions like stock or a returns policy. For account work, the customer signs in on the company's own page and grants read access, write access or both.

The phone is the hard case. A voice agent calling your front desk carries no signature. Treat it like any caller asking about someone else's account: share public information freely, and verify anything personal through the customer of record, for example a confirmation link or code sent to the phone number or email you already have on file.

What should an agent be allowed to do?

Write this down as policy before the first agent asks. Most businesses already have rules for staff, such as discount limits and refund approvals. Agent callers need the same rules, sorted by how much you know about who is behind the request.

Who is askingAllowedNeeds approvalNever
Unverified agent (phone, chat, signed-out session)Hours, services, published prices, availability, policiesHolding a slot that blocks other customersAccount details, personal data, changes
Agent with read access granted by the customerOrder status, upcoming appointments, balances on the customer's own accountSharing documents or recordsChanges of any kind
Agent with write access granted by the customerBooking, rescheduling and cancelling inside your normal policyRefunds, discounts or exceptions above your limitsChanging payment details or the contact on file

The "never" column matters most. An agent with write access is still software following instructions, and the person behind it may not have meant what the agent understood. Keep anything that moves money or changes who controls the account behind a step the customer confirms directly.

Why do structured answers beat a better website?

Agents read your business the way a new employee reads a shared drive: fast and literal, and with no sense of what is out of date. If your cancellation policy says one thing on the website and another in the booking confirmation, an agent will quote whichever it found first.

Meta put it bluntly in its announcement: "A personal agent should not have to interpret a support center article" (quoted in CMSWire). Start with one source of truth for the facts agents ask about most:

  • hours, locations and service areas;
  • prices, or price ranges with what changes them;
  • availability that comes from your real calendar;
  • cancellation, refund and rescheduling rules, with their thresholds.

Your own AI agent should answer from the same source. Then a customer's agent gets the same answer whether it reads your API, chats with your agent or calls the front desk.

What happens when the agent needs a person?

Some requests should reach a human: a complaint, an exception, anything with judgment in it. The Personal Agent Protocol draft builds this in. A personal agent can ask the company's agent for a person, the conversation waits in a queue until someone joins, and every message is tagged as written by the agent or by the human user. The company can also ask to speak with the user, but only the personal agent can bring the user in, so the customer decides when to join.

Whatever standard settles, the business side is the same. Hand off with the full history, so your staff member does not start from zero. And keep track of whose words are whose. "The customer said they want a refund" and "the agent decided the customer wants a refund" are not the same thing when there is a dispute.

What should you record for every agent request?

Gartner warns that AI assistants could make contacting a company nearly effortless, which likely means more requests, and calls that a cost risk to service teams (Gartner). More volume calls for a better record as well as more capacity. For each request from an agent, log:

  1. which agent made the request, and whether its identity was verified;
  2. which customer it acted for, and what access the customer had granted;
  3. what it asked for and what your system did;
  4. the rule that applied, and who approved it if approval was needed;
  5. whether a person took over, and when.

How to prepare your business for AI agents: a checklist

  1. Write the allowed / needs approval / never policy for agent callers, by level of verification.
  2. Brief the front desk on agent calls: share public information, verify everything personal through the customer.
  3. Put hours, prices, availability and policies in one source that your website, your staff and your own AI agent all use.
  4. Look at the agent traffic you already get, such as calls asking about someone else's booking.
  5. Decide which tasks you would offer agents directly first. Status checks and rescheduling are good candidates.
  6. Ask your software vendors what they plan for agent identity and the Personal Agent Protocol.
  7. Make sure handoffs to a person carry the full history.
  8. Log agent requests with the same detail as staff actions.

Where does an AI operating system fit?

An agent from the outside is easier to handle when your side already runs on rules. In an AI operating system for business, every request passes through the same layers whoever sends it: understand the request, decide under your rules, then act inside your systems and record it.

That is how we built Aurora. You choose what Aurora does on its own, what needs a person's approval and what it never does. Every action is logged with the rule that applied and who approved it, and your team can take over any conversation with the full history. The protocols for agent-to-agent service are still drafts. The rules and records you set now will carry over to whichever standard wins.

Frequently asked questions

Do I need to support the Personal Agent Protocol now?

Not yet for most businesses. The Personal Agent Protocol is at Draft 0.1, and its authors say any part can change before a stable version. The useful work now is the policy, the single source of facts and the logging, which apply to agents on any route.

Can I stop AI agents from calling my business?

You can limit some of them. Google says businesses can turn off its automated calls in Business Profile settings, under advanced settings, or ask the caller to stop calling (Google Business Profile Help). Other agents have no such switch, so a clear policy for agent callers is the more reliable answer.

Should an AI agent be allowed to change a customer's booking?

An AI agent can change a booking when the customer has granted write access and the change fits your normal policy. Without verified access, the agent should only receive public information, and any change should be confirmed by the customer directly.

Will agent-to-agent service replace talking to customers?

Agent-to-agent service will handle routine tasks such as status checks, bookings and simple questions. Complaints, exceptions and judgment calls still need a person, which is why a clean handoff with the full history matters on both sides.

Next steps

The fastest way to prepare your business for AI agents is the policy table and the checklist above. They take an afternoon, and nothing about them depends on which protocol wins. To see how rules, approvals and the audit log work in practice, explore the Aurora platform or read about how Aurora keeps you in control. If phone calls are your busiest channel, our guide to AI answering services for contractors shows how calls get triaged and booked.
